title: TESS CPV host M dwarfs have no extra H-alpha or X-ray emission compared with 1,504 matched rapid rotators, and APOGEE line widths of 18 hosts show spin axes near edge-on
abstract: We test whether complex periodic variable (CPV) host status in young M-dwarf rapid rotators comes from more corotating material or from viewing geometry. We use 1,837 TESS rapid rotators (117 on-target hosts) from earlier campaign work. (1) Gaia DR3 ESP-ELS H-alpha pseudo-equivalent widths: at fixed age class, colour, period, main-sequence height and G, 116 hosts do not have more emission than 1,504 matched non-hosts. The bias-corrected difference is +0.26 A (95% CI -0.04 to +0.56; positive is less emission). Extra emission in hosts is below 0.7-2.0% of the chromospheric emission component (95%). Host-only plasma that emits 10-60% of the stellar H-alpha, as spectra of single CPVs show, is excluded. Young and RUWE < 1.4 hosts have 7-9% less emission (2.4-3.0 sigma). (2) eROSITA eRASS1: hosts and non-hosts have the same detection odds and X-ray to optical flux ratio (difference -0.02 dex, 95% CI -0.07 to +0.03). (3) APOGEE DR17 v sin i with TIC radii: all 18 hosts (8 TESS, 10 K2 in Upper Sco and rho Oph) have v sin i / (2 pi R/P) above 0.9 (median 1.36), against 0.88 for 119 non-hosts, which agree with random orientations (Mann-Whitney p = 1e-9). A scale-free test finds the host values as narrow as the measurement scatter (p = 0.012 for random orientations). Thus host status follows mainly from an edge-on view of material near the rotational equator, not from more emitting plasma. Geometry alone does not explain the age decline of the host fraction. Limitations: one H-alpha pipeline (our own XP index failed as a check); Gaia spectra are from 2014-2017; the inclination sample is small and mostly 1-12 Myr; with the scale fixed by non-hosts, host ratios exceed the edge-on value by about 25%, which a common radius or v sin i scale error or extra broadening must explain.
